title: Grenache
description: Also called Garnacha in Spain and Cannonau in Sardinia. Red fruit, spice and warmth, from Châteauneuf to Priorat.
L: Grenache gives medium to full-bodied reds with strawberry, raspberry, red cherry, white pepper, dried herbs and, with age, leather and toffee. Colour is often paler than expected. Tannins are soft to medium, acidity low to medium, and alcohol high, often 14.5 to 16%.

Grenache, Garnacha in Spain, probably comes from Aragón, in north-east Spain; some argue for Sardinia, where it's called Cannonau. It loves heat and drought, and accumulates sugar fast, which explains its high alcohol. Thin skins mean paler colour and softer tannin. It oxidises easily, so it browns early.
Why is Grenache often high in alcohol?
It accumulates sugar quickly in heat
Grenache ripens to high sugar levels, which become alcohol.

Look for medium ruby colour, often with an orange rim early, ripe red fruit, white pepper and herbs, a warm, high-alcohol feel and soft tannins. Compared with Syrah, it's paler and redder-fruited; compared with Pinot Noir, warmer and riper.
Grenache usually gives deeply coloured, tannic wines.
Not true. Its thin skins give paler colour and softer tannin.
Grenache gives strawberry, spice and high alcohol
It comes from Spain and loves heat and drought
Thin skins mean paler colour and soft tannin
Explain why old bush vines matter

Grenache is one of the world's most planted red grapes. In France, it leads the southern Rhône and much of the Languedoc-Roussillon and Provence rosé. In Spain, it grows in Aragón, Navarra, Priorat, Rioja and around Madrid. Sardinia's Cannonau, Australia's Barossa and McLaren Vale, and California also grow it.

Grenache has strong, upright wood, so it's often grown as free-standing bush vines, gobelet. They need no trellis and withstand wind. Old bush vines, some over 100 years, with deep roots, survive drought and give low yields of concentrated fruit. Many of Grenache's best wines come from them.
Match each place to its Grenache.
Grenache thrives across warm, dry regions.

Grenache brings red fruit, body and alcohol to blends. Syrah adds colour and structure; Mourvèdre adds tannin and savoury notes; Carignan adds acidity. Rioja adds Garnacha to Tempranillo. Its low colour and tendency to oxidise make it a natural team player.
Grenache ripens easily; it's rarely unripe.
Grenache is one of the most planted red grapes
Old bush vines give concentrated wines
It's a team player in GSM and Rioja blends

Châteauneuf-du-Pape, near Avignon, was named after the 14th century popes' summer castle. It allows 13 grape varieties, but Grenache usually leads, often 70% or more. Its famous galets roulés, large round stones, store heat and reflect light. In 1923, Baron Le Roy's rules there helped inspire France's AOC system.

Gigondas and Vacqueyras, nearby, make powerful Grenache-led reds. Côtes du Rhône and Côtes du Rhône Villages offer more affordable versions. Château Rayas is a famous Châteauneuf made almost entirely from Grenache, on sandy soil, showing the grape's elegance.
What are the galets roulés of Châteauneuf-du-Pape?
Large round stones that store heat
These river stones store heat by day and release it at night.

Grenache is the main grape of many rosés: Provence, Tavel and Navarra's rosado. Its thin skins give pale colour quickly, and its red fruit and body suit dry rosé. Tavel, in the southern Rhône, is a rosé-only appellation, fuller and darker than Provence.
Not true. It allows 13 varieties, though Grenache usually leads.
Châteauneuf-du-Pape is Grenache-led, with galets and 13 grapes
Gigondas, Vacqueyras and Côtes du Rhône follow
Grenache is key to Provence, Tavel and Navarra rosé

In Aragón, Garnacha's likely birthplace, Campo de Borja, Calatayud and Cariñena have many old bush vines on poor, stony soils. Campo de Borja calls itself the empire of Garnacha. These areas once made bulk wine but now offer concentrated, good-value Garnacha.

In Priorat, old Garnacha and Cariñena on llicorella slate make powerful, mineral wines. In the Sierra de Gredos, west of Madrid, old Garnacha vines on granite at 600 to 1,200 m were rediscovered in the 2000s. Gredos Garnacha is pale, fragrant and fresh, often compared with Burgundy.
Match each Spanish area to its Garnacha.
Spain shows every side of Garnacha.
Gredos Garnacha shows a lighter, more elegant face of the grape. Try one next to a Châteauneuf to see how much altitude and granite change it.
Why is Gredos Garnacha often fresher than other Garnachas?
Altitude up to 1,200 m and granite give freshness and perfume.
Aragón is Garnacha's homeland, with old bush vines
Priorat makes powerful Garnacha on slate
Gredos makes fragrant, fresh Garnacha at altitude
Explain how sweet Grenache is made

In Roussillon, Grenache makes vins doux naturels: spirit is added during fermentation, stopping it and keeping natural sugar. Grenache's high sugar and red fruit suit this. Banyuls and Maury are the most famous red ones, also Rivesaltes. They have 15 to 18% alcohol.

Banyuls and Maury are made in two styles. Rimage or grenat styles are bottled young, keeping red fruit, like ruby Port. Traditional styles age with oxygen for years, in barrels or in glass demijohns left in the sun, giving notes of nuts, coffee, dried fruit and rancio, a complex, nutty, oxidative character.
A nutty, oxidative character from long ageing
Rancio develops in wines aged with oxygen and heat.

Banyuls and Maury are among the few wines that match dark chocolate. Rimage styles suit red fruit desserts; aged styles suit coffee, walnut and caramel desserts, and blue cheese. Serve slightly cool, around 14 to 16 degrees.
Which are sweet fortified Grenache wines?
Banyuls and Maury are fortified Grenache from Roussillon
Rimage is fresh; traditional styles age with oxygen
They're rare partners for dark chocolate

Grenache's ripe fruit and soft tannin suit roast lamb, Provençal stews, grilled sausages, roast pork and dishes with herbs and garlic. Lighter Gredos styles suit roast chicken and mushrooms. Its sweetness of fruit handles mildly spicy food, though high alcohol can clash with chilli.

Serve at 15 to 17 degrees; high alcohol feels hot if served too warm. Simple Côtes du Rhône and Garnacha are best within three years. Top Châteauneuf and Priorat age 15 to 25 years, though Grenache browns early, so colour isn't a reliable guide to age.
Why should Grenache not be served too warm?
Warmth makes high alcohol more noticeable.
A slightly cool Grenache rosé from Provence is one of the most versatile summer wines, from salads to grilled fish.
Top Châteauneuf-du-Pape can age 15 to 25 years.
Yes, especially from top producers and vintages.
Grenache suits lamb, stews and herby dishes
Top Châteauneuf and Priorat age for decades
